children: Iron ore futures rose on Monday, supported by higher freight and oil costs, though surging coking coal prices squeezed steel mill margins and capped gains.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
closed morning trade 0.35% higher at 724 yuan ($107.73) a metric ton.
The benchmark September iron ore (SZZFU6) on the Singapore Exchange was 0.65% higher at $99.2 a ton.

Oil prices were trading more than 2% higher after the U.S. attacked an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz and drew retaliation from Tehran, as conflict in the Middle East extended into its sixth month.
Rising oil prices and shipping costs have formed a bottom support for iron ore prices, analysts from Chinese broker Everbright Futures said in a note.
However, rising coking coal prices continue to squeeze steel mill profits, limiting further upside in hot iron output and leaving mills with little incentive to restock, the analysts said.

The blast furnace operating rate among 247 steel mills fell to 82.32% last week, down 0.48 percentage points, while daily hot iron output slipped 10,800 tons to 2.37 million tons, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.
China's non-manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI), which covers services and construction, remained unchanged at 49.0, matching July's reading, the weakest since December 2022.
Sweeping regulatory changes for China's crisis-hit property sector announced last week sent shares in smaller developers sharply lower amid expectations of more industry consolidation.
